author: haiku
label: seeded-01-01
changes: Rewrote the document as a full design. The original was a stub: its diagram showed only the happy path and its notes were bare labels.
Added the 401 branch, so the diagram shows that a bad key is rejected before any counter is touched.
Added the Redis outcome branches: over limit (429 with Retry-After, no budget used), under limit (forwarded and counted), and fail open (on error or 50 ms timeout).
Put the 50 ms budget on the Redis call in the diagram, so the fail-open condition is visible.
Stated the per-customer counter explicitly, so it is clear that keys share one budget.
Explained why the Lua script prevents overshoot across instances, and why a rejected request uses no budget.
Defined the window: 60 seconds, starting at the first counted request, with the TTL controlling expiry.
Defined how Retry-After is calculated, and why every instance gives the same value.
Stated the window-boundary trade-off (up to 200 requests in a few seconds) as a known first-version limitation.
Noted that a backend 500 still uses budget, because the count happens before forwarding.
Made the Enterprise limit visibly open, with a rule not to ship it until Product decides.
Noted the 5-minute key cache, which delays plan changes.
Defined the fail-open response: no X-RateLimit headers, plus the metric. Stated that limits are not enforced during an outage.
Kept the Mermaid sequenceDiagram format and the short notes below it.
Added a short list of terms (customer, gateway, Redis, window, fail open) before the diagram so a reader new to the project knows what the words mean.
Renamed the diagram label from '50 ms budget' to '50 ms timeout' to say plainly what the 50 ms limit is.
Grouped the notes under plain labels (who is counted, order of checks, shared counting, no overshoot, window, Retry-After, fail open) so each design point is easy to find.
Explained what a Lua script is in one clause and why it prevents two instances from both allowing the 100th request.
Explained TTL on first use and what happens when the key expires, so the fixed window is clear without prior knowledge.
Rewrote the fixed-window trade-off as a concrete example (100 at the end of one window plus 100 at the start of the next).
Stated explicitly that a 401 reads and changes no counter, and that the check runs before forwarding.
Changed 'Enterprise is TBD, pending a Product decision' to 'to be decided by Product' and kept the rule not to ship an Enterprise limit until it is set.
Put the 5-minute plan-change delay under its own label, and kept the fail-open trade-off visible.
Expanded the terms list to define API key, Plan, Key Service, Backend, and Gateway as a single entry point, so a reader outside the project can follow the diagram.
Stated at the top that the Enterprise limit is not set and not implemented.
Added the 5-minute key lookup cache to the diagram's Key Service call and to the notes, and explained the effect on plan changes.
Labeled the 401 branch as making no Redis call in the diagram.
Added a note to the fail-open branch of the diagram for the ratelimit_store_unavailable metric, which was previously only in the prose.
Explained the check_and_incr Lua script in plain terms: it adds 1 and allows only when the count is below the limit, and otherwise adds nothing.
Defined TTL in the window note and clarified that the first counted request creates the counter.
Reworded the Redis-allowed message in the diagram to show the count is increased before the response returns.
Merged the duplicated Enterprise wording and kept the rule that no Enterprise limit ships until Product sets it.
